title: Sugar Prices Jump Over 10% in Six Days as Diwali Demand Meets Tight Stocks
excerpt: Ex-mill prices are up nearly Rs 1,000 a quintal in ten days and Delhi retail has touched Rs 65 a kg, prompting the government to rush out a 16 lakh tonne sales quota before Diwali on November 8.
body:
• Sugar prices have risen more than 10% in six days, with ex-mill rates in Uttar Pradesh jumping to Rs 5,400 a quintal from about Rs 4,450 ten days ago.
  • Delhi retail prices have touched Rs 65 a kg in some markets, up from Rs 60, as festive buying peaks ahead of Diwali on November 8.
  • The government has brought forward a 16 lakh tonne sales quota for October 13-31 — 14 lakh tonnes from domestic mills and 2 lakh tonnes from importers — to cool the market.
  • Any relief hinges on new-season crushing, which has begun in Maharashtra, because traders say stocks left at mills are close to negligible.

Sugar has turned sharply more expensive in the middle of India's festival season. Prices have risen more than 10% in six days amid tight supplies ahead of Diwali, the Hindustan Times reported, and market data point the same way: ex-mill prices have climbed nearly Rs 1,000 a quintal in ten days, according to The Hindu BusinessLine. In Uttar Pradesh, the country's largest producing state, ex-mill sugar was quoted at Rs 5,400 a quintal, up from about Rs 4,450 ten days earlier. Maharashtra mills were quoting around Rs 5,100 a quintal.

Why Prices Are Spiking

Demand for sugar in India rises every year between August and November, when Ganesh Chaturthi, Dussehra and Diwali drive sweets and confectionery production. This year the demand peak has met a thin cupboard. Production last season fell short of annual consumption, and opening stocks for the new marketing year were expected at around 3.5 million tonnes — the lowest in more than 30 years — after exports of about 800,000 tonnes, traders told Reuters. The government has already banned sugar exports and tightened stockholding limits, ordering bulk consumers who use more than 10 tonnes a month to hold no more than 15 days of inventory from September 1 to November 30.

"Demand has started increasing ahead of the festive season, while sugar mills are releasing stocks gradually because they expect prices to rise further."

— Ashok Jain, President, Bombay Sugar Merchants Association

That slow release is part of the problem. Some mills exhausted their sales quota for October 1-15 and could not sell at all, officials said, and word of the empty quotas fuelled speculation that stocks were running out — pushing prices higher still.

Government Moves Early With a Festival Quota

The Food Ministry has allocated 16 lakh tonnes for sale between October 13 and 31, announcing the quota two days early because of the price spurt. Of that, 14 lakh tonnes go to domestic mills and 2 lakh tonnes to importers. The top three producing states account for 11.59 lakh tonnes of the domestic allocation — Maharashtra 4.76 lakh tonnes, Uttar Pradesh 4.51 lakh tonnes and Karnataka 2.32 lakh tonnes. Of 587 mills, 134 received no allocation at all, while refiners Shree Renuka Sugars and Shri Dutt India were allotted 1.30 lakh tonnes and 70,000 tonnes respectively against imported sugar.

The Tight Arithmetic Behind the Rally

The numbers explain the official urgency. India's closing stock on September 30 was estimated at 32-35 lakh tonnes. Excluding imported sugar, domestic mills have been allocated 27 lakh tonnes for October alone, and November demand is expected at another 24-25 lakh tonnes. Trade sources estimate India needs 12-13 lakh tonnes of production in October itself to carry the market through November. The new crushing season has started — about 30 mills in Maharashtra are crushing and 10 more are expected within days, while 10-15 mills in Uttar Pradesh should start around October 20 — but until crushing hits full pace, supply stays tight. Dussehra demand on October 20 is largely covered; Diwali, on November 8, is the real test.

What It Means for Households

Retail prices are following wholesale rates up. In Delhi, sugar has inched to Rs 65 a kg in some markets from Rs 60 within days, though many outlets have yet to reprice. In Hyderabad, traders quoted sugar at Rs 53-55 a kg on October 12, up from Rs 46-48 in September, as part of a broader festival-season rise in staples. Sweet and snack makers have reported sugar procurement costs running well above levels of a few months ago, which is why mithai counters are repricing ahead of Diwali. For diaspora households, the pass-through arrives through Indian grocery imports and festive sweet orders: buy Diwali sugar and mithai supplies early where you can, because Indian market relief is not expected until new-season crushing builds up in November.
